messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: plot type l?
parts:
I think the NA's are killing you. In fact, you *do* get a line on
your 'l' plot, but it's not the line you want.

Something like this might help:

library(dplyr)

tet %>%
filter(!is.na(x)) -> tet_clean

plot(tet_clean$x)
plot(tet_clean$x, type = 'l')

> but when to plot it as line, I do:
> plot(tet$x,type="l")
>
> but nothing appear on the plot it is empty. I tried lines but no success.
> ANy idea?
> Bic

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: plot type l?
parts:
Here's one answer to the question:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rtEaR1JU-ps

I was skeptical of the Hadley approach at first, and I'm still
uncomfortable with some of the side effects of NSE. I can probably
dig up some examples where I went through tutorials on the Hadley
stuff and tried to work out how to do the same thing in "real" R.
And, so far as I know, it's always possible. Be careful of strings as
factors, for instance. Renumber the output lines. Etc.

OTOH, when a large number of very-smart people on this list started
giving responses based on dplyr, etc., I decided to try to go with the
flow. (Duncan and Matt being examples of very-smart people who have
consistently taken the "real-R" approach, by the way.)

I've now gone with flow to a sufficient degree that using "filter" and
friends was the first thing that came to my mind. But, as Brandon
observes, you get the essentially the same results either way.

-- Mike

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: plot type l?
parts:
filter is possibly one of the less interesting/innovative function in the dplyr/tidyverse, which has much more to offer. 

Besides readability, an important difference however is that subsetting a data-frame with [,] is not necessarily output-stable: you might end-up with a data-frame, or a simple numeric value. Recasting it into a data-frame as you do does the job, though colnames change, and probably not efficient. filter() will always return a data frame. 

df <- data.frame(var=c(NA, 1,2))
as.data.frame(df[!is.na(df$var),])
filter(df, !is.na(a))

dig up some examples where I went through tutorials on the Hadley
stuff and tried to work out how to do the same thing in "real" R.
And, so far as I know, it's always possible.  Be careful of strings as
factors, for instance.  Renumber the output lines.  Etc.

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: plot type l?
parts:
Hi

I have no desire to advocate for [] or filter. I just want to ensure that no misconception gets propagated for the future.
Subsetting with [ ] can ensure a data frame with  drop = FALSE, e.g.,
    df[, 1, drop = FALSE]
and more generally the same for a matrix.

And just for reference, I note that sometimes you *want* to end up
with a vector at the end of a dplyr (or other) chain of pipes. I
looked this up a couple of years ago, and Hadley had replied (on SO)
that such-and-such was the obvious way to do this. It wasn't at all
obvious to me. OTOH, I note that since that time Hadley has added a
function to do this, as:

library(dplyr)

> mtcars %>% pull(mpg)

[1] 21.0 21.0 22.8 21.4 18.7 18.1 14.3 24.4 22.8 19.2 17.8 16.4 17.3 15.2 10.4

[16] 10.4 14.7 32.4 30.4 33.9 21.5 15.5 15.2 13.3 19.2 27.3 26.0 30.4 15.8 19.7

[31] 15.0 21.4

>
